summary: RFC 6282 defines header compression for 6LoWPAN packets. This document adds a simple way to compress generic headers and header-like payloads, without a new compression scheme for each new one.

eli5.summary: Sending long messages over tiny wireless links is costly, so this RFC shrinks the repeated parts of headers. It works for lots of kinds of headers, not just one.

questions: how does generic header compression work in 6lowpan
subtitle: A tiny bytecode that compresses almost any header or header-like payload on 6LoWPAN links.

tldr.problem: 6LoWPAN header compression needs a new specification for each new kind of header, so the scheme kept being reopened whenever a header was added or changed.
tldr.mechanism: 6LoWPAN-GHC defines a simple LZ77-style bytecode, plugged in as Next Header Compression formats for UDP, ICMPv6 and extension headers, with a predefined dictionary built from the packet's IPv6 addresses and a 16-byte static dictionary. A new Neighbor Discovery option, the 6CIO, tells neighbors that a node can decode it.
tldr.outcome: It is slightly less efficient than a purpose-built format but works for headers of any kind. Its security section warns about decompression bombs and forged capability claims.

today: RFC 7400 is a Proposed Standard. No later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: The Coupling Problem
sections.content:
RFC 6282 defines 6LoWPAN Header Compression (6LoWPAN-HC) for IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Networks. Like most header compression schemes, it needs a new specification for every new header, and it has no extensibility scheme like the ROHC profiles. As a result it tended to be reopened each time a header was added or changed.

This RFC plugs into RFC 6282 as is, using its Next Header Compression (NHC) concept. It adds Generic Header Compression (GHC): slightly less efficient but far more general, covering headers of any kind and header-like payloads such as those of routing protocols and DHCP. The goal is a specification that fits on one page and takes a small number of lines of code, unlike a general data compression scheme such as RFC 1951.
sections.eli5: Normally every new kind of message needs its own special shrinking rules. GHC is one all-purpose shrinking trick, so nobody has to keep inventing new rules.

sections.title: The GHC Bytecode
sections.content:
The approach is a bytecode for LZ77-style compression. A compressed header is a sequence of pieces, each starting with a code byte that may be followed by an argument. The decompressor has two variables, sa and na, set to zero at the start of each packet fragment.

The instructions are: append up to 95 literal bytes (0kkkkkkk), append a run of zero bytes (1000nnnn), set up extended arguments for a backreference (101nssss), copy bytes from earlier output (11nnnkkk), and a stop code (10010000). The patterns 011xxxxx and 1001nnnn with a non-zero nnnn are reserved.

Backreferences may reach into a predefined dictionary placed before the payload. It holds the source and destination IPv6 addresses of the packet, followed by a 16-byte static dictionary. These 48 bytes can be copied from but are not part of the output. The RFC specifies the decompressor in detail and leaves the compressor to implementers.
sections.eli5: The shorthand has a few instructions: 'write these letters', 'write some zeros', and 'copy what you wrote a little while ago'. It also starts with a small cheat sheet of things most messages contain.

sections.title: Plugging Into 6LoWPAN-HC
sections.content:
GHC is added as NHC formats. For UDP, the NHC byte is 11010CPP, analogous to the existing 11110CPP but with the UDP payload compressed by GHC instead of supplied literally. For ICMPv6 a single byte, 11011111, is used.

Extension headers get 10110EEN. Their Length field is elided and rebuilt on decompression, so the stop code 10010000 is needed to mark where the compressed extension header ends. Final payloads such as UDP and ICMPv6 end with the packet, so they need no stop code.
sections.eli5: Each kind of packet gets a short label saying 'this one was shrunk with the all-purpose trick'. Packets that are not the last part also get a stop sign so the reader knows where to quit.

sections.title: Finding Out Who Understands GHC
sections.content:
A node should only send GHC-compressed packets to a neighbor that implements GHC. Capability can be required administratively, learned implicitly by receiving a GHC packet, or announced with the new 6LoWPAN Capability Indication Option (6CIO), a Neighbor Discovery option. Its G bit says the sender is GHC capable.

The 6CIO is typically sent in Router Solicitations. The Router Advertisement reply can then use GHC, which signals capability implicitly and lets both sides use GHC in Neighbor Solicitation and Advertisement. Where capability is not recently confirmed, a node SHOULD use Neighbor Unreachability Detection failures to fall back to basic RFC 6282 compression.

Unassigned bits MUST be sent as zero and ignored on receipt. Flag numbers 0 to 7 are reserved for experimental use and MUST NOT be used in real deployments. Lengths greater than 1 MUST be accepted for future extensions.
sections.eli5: Before using the shorthand, you check that the other side can read it. A node can say 'I speak it' in a hello message, or the other side can notice it when it receives a shortened message.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content: IANA added the three NHC bytes to the LOWPAN_NHC Header Type registry, allocated Neighbor Discovery option number 36 for the 6CIO, and created a '6LoWPAN capability Bits' subregistry covering bits 0 to 47. The policy is IETF Review or IESG Approval. Bits 0-7 are experimental, bit 15 is the G bit, and the rest are unassigned.
sections.eli5: The official number registry now lists the new labels so nobody uses them for something else.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 4944 and RFC 6282 apply. Implementations must avoid buffer overflows and out-of-area backreferences during decompression.

A forged packet could make a node believe a victim is GHC capable, so packets to the victim may be lost until fallback kicks in. No mitigation is known, but a victim that implements GHC is not vulnerable.

As with any LZ77 scheme, decompression bombs are possible. The RFC gives the worst-case amplification of GHC as 17, so an MTU-size packet can come from a 6LoWPAN packet of 76 bytes. Network access control mitigates these attacks. A deployment relying only on MAC-layer security could also leak secrets through compression redundancy, which is avoided by not exposing secrets to the adaptation layer or not using GHC there.
sections.eli5: A sneaky sender could pack a tiny note that unfolds into a giant one and overwhelm the reader. Careful readers check limits, and a locked network keeps strangers out.

items.label: Literal bytes
items.desc: Append k bytes of data given in the argument (k < 96).

items.label: Extended arguments
items.desc: Set up sa and na for a backreference.

items.label: Backreference
items.desc: Copy n bytes from previously output bytes, then reset sa and na.
